paragraphs.source_en: Behind my house there is a tea garden of about ten tsubo. It is not a large place, but it is neat, pleasant, and well blessed with sunlight. Whenever the children of the house make such a racket that I cannot take my afternoon nap in comfort, or whenever I am bored to death and out of sorts in the stomach, I always come here to restore my ample spirit. One day in October, in the mild weather of an Indian summer, with warm sun and gentle wind, at about two in the afternoon, after finishing lunch and enjoying a thoroughly satisfying nap, I strolled out into the tea garden to stretch my limbs. Sniffing at the roots of each tea shrub, one by one, I came to the cedar hedge on the west side. There I saw a large black cat lying on a flattened clump of withered chrysanthemums, sleeping with its head buried. When I drew near, it seemed not to notice me at all; or, if it did notice, it paid me no mind, but lay there at ease, still snoring loudly. That one should sneak into another creature's garden and sleep with such utter unconcern could not help but astonish me by its boldness. It was a black cat without a trace of any other color. The sun, only just past noon, cast transparent, dazzling rays upon its skin, so that from among its soft fur there seemed to flicker a flame invisible to the eye. It possessed a magnificent body worthy of being called a king among cats, fully twice the size of my own. Lost in admiration and curiosity, I forgot everything and stood before it, gazing at it with complete absorption. Just then, the gentle breeze of that mild autumn day lightly stirred the thin branches of the paulownia that stretched over the cedar hedge, and two or three leaves fell sparsely into the withered chrysanthemum clump. The great lord suddenly opened its perfectly round eyes. Even now I remember those shining eyes, far more beautiful than the amber prized by human beings. It did not move a muscle, but gathered the sharp light shooting from the depths of both eyes upon my narrow little forehead. It interrogated me: “What in the world are you?” For a king, its diction was somewhat vulgar; nevertheless, in the depths of that voice there was a power enough to cow even a fierce dog, and I felt no small alarm. I thought it would be dangerous not to offer a few words of greeting. So, doing my utmost to appear unconcerned, I answered coolly, “I am a cat. I have as yet no name.” At that moment, however, my heart was certainly beating harder than usual. In an exceedingly contemptuous tone he said, “What? You are a cat too? The very thought of a cat like you makes me sick! Well then, where do you live?” Its manner was outrageously overbearing. “I live in this teacher's house.” I replied. It immediately retorted, “I thought it must be something like that. Just look at you, nothing but skin and bones!” As one would expect of a king of cats, its bearing was lofty and its tone aggressive. Judging from its way of speaking, it somehow did not seem to be a cat raised in a respectable household. Yet, looking at its glossy, fat body, it seemed to eat delicacies and to live in considerable prosperity. I could not help asking, “Then who, may I ask, are you?”

paragraphs.source_en: “I'm Kuro from the rickshaw man's place!” he answered with proud self-importance. When it comes to Kuro of the rickshaw man, there is no one in this neighborhood who does not know him; he is a thoroughly rough-and-tumble cat. But precisely because he belonged to a rickshaw man, he was all strength, bravado, and no education whatever, so hardly anyone associated with him. He was the sort of fellow whom everyone treated with respectful avoidance. As soon as I heard his name, I felt a slight uneasiness. At the same time, I also felt a little contempt for him. The first thing that occurred to me was to test just how ignorant and unlearned he was. Thus I had the following exchange with him:
